parts.title: Tuning the Casimir Force Between Graphene-Covered Hyperbolic Materials
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We propose a flexible way to change the Casimir force, a tiny pull between two surfaces that are very close together. Our method combines graphene, a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, with hyperbolic materials. These are materials that bend light and other waves in unusual ways. We use two different materials as the partner for graphene. The first is hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), a natural hyperbolic material. The second is porous silicon carbide (SiC), which is silicon carbide riddled with tiny air holes. Using a method called effective medium theory, which treats a material full of holes as if it were a single material with averaged properties, we can treat porous SiC as a man-made, or artificial, hyperbolic material.

We calculate the Casimir force between two solid blocks, each covered with graphene, one made of hBN and one made of porous SiC. We work at zero temperature, meaning no heat is present. We find that covering a hyperbolic material with graphene makes the Casimir force larger, and the force keeps growing steadily as the Fermi level goes up. The Fermi level is a setting in graphene that controls how many electrons are free to move. The force can also be tuned by changing the Fermi level, especially when the two blocks are far apart.

We look closely at the reflection coefficients, which describe how strongly each surface bounces back waves of different kinds. We trace the extra force to the way two kinds of waves interact. Graphene supports surface plasmons, which are ripples of electrons along its surface. The hyperbolic materials support hyperbolic phonon polaritons, which are waves that travel along the material's surface.

We also show that the Casimir force can be controlled by the filling factor of porous SiC, which is the share of the material taken up by air holes. So the Casimir force can be tuned flexibly by designing the right artificial hyperbolic materials and by adjusting the Fermi level. Our models look promising for practical detection and for technology.

Keywords: Casimir force, graphene, hyperbolic material
parts.introduction_first:
The Casimir force is a fascinating effect that shows up at a scale we can see, even though it comes from tiny, random jiggles in the electromagnetic field, the field that carries light and electricity. These jiggles are called quantum fluctuations. In 1948, Hendrik Casimir predicted that two perfectly conducting plates placed parallel to each other would attract each other [1]. Later, Evgeny Lifshitz built a more general theory. It covers two parallel plates of dielectric material, meaning material that does not conduct electricity, each extending without limit in one direction. His theory also allows the material to change how it responds to different colors of light and to absorb some of it, and it works at any temperature [2].

The Casimir effect is still a hot topic, especially as engineers build microelectromechanical and nanoelectromechanical systems (MEMS and NEMS). These are tiny machines with moving parts, some only millionths or billionths of a meter across. Over the last twenty years, researchers have focused on understanding the Casimir effect in theory [3,4,5,6] and on measuring it precisely [7,8,9,10,11,12,13].

In most studies, the Casimir force is set up between two parallel plates of natural materials, with a vacuum gap between them. Usually the force is too weak to detect in practice, so making it stronger is very important. The force is also usually attractive. It is strongest at distances smaller than a micrometer, a thousandth of a millimeter. At such distances, neighboring parts of MEMS and NEMS can stick together permanently [14,15,16]. For these reasons, being able to adjust the Casimir force matters both for basic science and for technology [5,17].

Whether the force pushes the plates apart instead of pulling them together depends on how the materials at the surfaces respond to electric and magnetic fields, and on how balanced those responses are [18,19]. This is why it has become an interesting question to use special materials whose electromagnetic properties can be controlled to adjust the Casimir force [4]. Metamaterials are one example. These are man-made materials with unusual electromagnetic properties that natural materials do not have. They have been used for cloaking [20], for making objects see-through using the vacuum [21], and for controlling the Casimir effect [22,23,24]. Other materials have also been proposed for adjusting the Casimir effect, such as saturated ferrites [25,26] and topological insulators [27,28,29].
parts.conclusion:
4. Conclusions

In this work, we studied the Casimir force between two identical blocks, each covered with graphene and each made of a hyperbolic material. In our first model, the blocks were solid hBN covered with graphene. When graphene covers hBN, the Casimir force grows larger at every separation distance. As the Fermi level (Ef) rises, the force keeps increasing steadily. We examined the reflection coefficients of these samples in detail. Surface plasmons on the graphene and hyperbolic phonon polaritons on the hBN interact with each other, and these waves are linked to the stronger Casimir force.

In our second model, we replaced the hBN with porous SiC, which we treated as an artificial hyperbolic material using effective medium theory. As the Fermi level rises, the Casimir force still increases steadily. However, as the filling factor (f), the share of the material taken up by air holes, increases, the force gets smaller at every separation distance. We used the way porous SiC responds to electromagnetic waves to explain this.

So, by designing suitable artificial hyperbolic materials and adjusting the Fermi level, we can control the Casimir force between graphene-covered hyperbolic materials. By combining graphene with a hyperbolic material, this work offers a flexible way to adjust the Casimir effect, which can be used to detect the Casimir force.
parts.introduction_rest:
Graphene has caught the interest of many scientists [30]. It is a sheet of carbon atoms just one atom thick, with the atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern of six-sided rings. Near a special energy called the Dirac point, graphene's electrons behave in an unusual way. Their energy rises in a straight line with their momentum, which is called a linear dispersion relation. This gives graphene an extraordinary response to light [31]. In particular, graphene can support surface plasmons, ripples of electrons along its surface, at frequencies from the terahertz range up to the infrared [32]. Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared light, and infrared light is just beyond the red light our eyes can see.

Researchers have also studied a great deal about using graphene to adjust the Casimir effect [32,33,34,35,36,37,38,39,40]. It is well known that the way graphene's surface plasmons respond depends strongly on the substrate, the material the graphene is placed on [41]. Because of this, scientists have used models with graphene to study several effects. One is the Goos-Hänchen shift, a tiny sideways shift in a light beam when it bounces off a surface [42,43]. Another is quantum interference, where waves add together or cancel out [44]. A third is Casimir friction, a drag force that appears when two surfaces slide past each other [32,33].

For example, covering a hyperbolic material with graphene can greatly increase Casimir friction [33]. This happens because the surface plasmons on the graphene link up with the hyperbolic phonon polaritons that the hyperbolic material supports. The boost is active, meaning it can be switched on and off. That is because graphene's optical conductivity, which describes how easily it carries electric current in response to light, can be adjusted with an outside electric field or with a gate voltage, the voltage used to control a device.

Over the last ten years, hyperbolic materials have drawn a lot of attention because of their unusual electromagnetic properties [45]. To see why, it helps to know about permittivity. This is a set of numbers that describes how a material responds to an electric field. In a uniaxial hyperbolic material, the material behaves differently along one special direction than along the other two. For this material, the numbers along the two ordinary directions have opposite signs. As a result, for TM polarization, where the electric field lies in the plane of the surface, the set of waves with the same frequency forms a hyperbola instead of a circle [46]. This shape is called an isofrequency contour.

Hyperbolic materials can carry waves with very large wave vectors, which means waves that are squeezed into very small spaces. They can also support waves that travel along their surface. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a natural hyperbolic material that behaves this way in the infrared [47]. hBN can support hyperbolic phonon polaritons, and these have been studied in depth [48]. As technology for making tiny structures improves, people can also build artificial hyperbolic materials that behave this way in chosen frequency bands.

Artificial hyperbolic materials can be made in two main ways. One is by stacking layers of metal and dielectric material [49]. The other is by placing a grid of nanowires, which are extremely thin wires, inside a dielectric material [46]. The ingredients and how much of each is used can be chosen to give the material the electromagnetic properties we want. So, compared with natural hyperbolic materials, artificial ones offer extra ways to adjust hyperbolic phonon polaritons.

It is well known that the electromagnetic properties of the material at the surface can change the Casimir force [6]. In this paper, we study the Casimir force between two blocks, each covered with graphene and each made of a hyperbolic material. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the two models we consider and the Casimir force between two graphene-covered hyperbolic materials. Section 3 shows how the Casimir force can be adjusted when surface plasmons and hyperbolic phonon polaritons interact. Our results show that the Casimir force can be actively adjusted by the Fermi level and by artificial hyperbolic materials. Section 4 gives our conclusions.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods

Figure 1 shows our plan, which uses two different models. In each model, we study the Casimir force between two identical blocks separated by a distance d. In the first model, the blocks are solid hBN covered with graphene (Figure 1a). In the second, they are porous SiC covered with graphene (Figure 1b). Both models sit in free space, with the flat x−y plane lying parallel to the graphene sheet.

To describe how graphene responds to light, we use its conductivity, σ. This is how easily electric current flows within the graphene sheet. We work at low frequencies and with a high doping limit, meaning the graphene holds a large number of extra electrons. In this case, the conductivity can be written as [42]

(1) σ(ω) = i e² EF / (π ℏ² (ω + i/τ)),

using a standard simplifying assumption called the random phase approximation (RPA). Here, e is the electric charge of an electron, and EF is the Fermi level. The symbol ω stands for the frequency of the light, and ℏ is a fixed number from quantum physics. The quantity τ is the relaxation time, which describes how quickly moving electrons lose their motion. It is caused by the extra electrons, by defects in the material, and by phonons, which are tiny vibrations of the atoms. It is given by τ = μ EF / (e vF²). The mobility μ describes how easily the charge carriers move through graphene, and it is μ = 10⁴−10⁶ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. The Fermi velocity vF, the typical speed of these electrons, is vF = 10⁶ m/s.

Figure 1

The Casimir force between two graphene-covered hyperbolic materials separated by a distance d. The two models are (a) graphene-covered hBN and (b) graphene-covered porous SiC.

hBN is naturally anisotropic, which means its properties depend on the direction you look at it. It also shows hyperbolic dispersion, a special way of bending waves. Its permittivity, ε, describes how strongly a material responds to an electric field. Because hBN is anisotropic, the permittivity is a tensor, a set of numbers that gives a different value for each direction. Its values are [33]

(2) εl,hBN = εl,∞ [1 + (ωLO,l² − ωTO,l²)/(ωTO,l² − ω² − iωγl)],

where l = xx or zz, meaning the direction of the field. LO and TO are two kinds of phonon vibration, and γ is the damping coefficient, which describes how quickly the vibration dies away. The values are εxx,∞ = 4.87, ωLO,xx = 3.0348 ω0, ωTO,xx = 2.5824 ω0, γxx = 0.0094 ω0, εzz,∞ = 2.95, ωLO,zz = 1.5645 ω0, ωTO,zz = 1.4703 ω0, and γzz = 0.0075 ω0. Here ω0 = 10¹⁴ rad/s is a reference frequency.

Figure 2a plots the real parts of εl,hBN against ω. The real part is the part of the permittivity that stores energy rather than absorbing it. Two grey shaded zones appear where Re εxx Re εzz < 0, that is, where the real parts in the two directions have opposite signs. In these zones, hyperbolic phonon polaritons can be excited. Electromagnetic waves in such zones carry a large wave vector, which means they are very tightly packed in space. As a result, the electromagnetic local density of states, a measure of how many wave states are available in a small region, becomes very large [46].

Figure 2

(a) The real parts of εl,hBN plotted against ω. (b) The real parts of εl,p−SiC plotted against ω with a filling factor f = 0.3. Here l = xx or zz, and the grey shaded zones mark the hyperbolic bands. The small inset shows the real parts of εl,p−SiC from 1.72 ω0 to 1.84 ω0.

Bulk SiC is isotropic, so it responds the same way in every direction. Its permittivity can be described by the Lorentz model [40]

(3) εs(ω) = ε∞ (ω² − ωL² + iγω)/(ω² − ωT² + iγω),

where ε∞ = 6.7, ωL = 1.827 ω0, ωT = 1.495 ω0, and γ = 0.009 ω0.

To give the material the anisotropy we want, we can build a lattice of nanowires, tiny wires a billionth of a meter across, set in a dielectric background. In the same way, we can make an artificial hyperbolic material by placing a lattice of air cylinders inside SiC. Using the Maxwell-Garnett method [50], a standard way of averaging the properties of a material full of holes, the effective permittivity of this porous SiC is

(4) εxx,p−SiC = εyy,p−SiC = [(1 + f) + (1 − f)εs] εs / [(1 − f) + (1 + f)εs],

(5) εzz,p−SiC = f + (1 − f)εs,

where f is the filling factor. It is the percentage of the area in the xy cross-section of the material taken up by air holes. Figure 2b shows the real parts of εl,p−SiC (l = xx or zz) against ω for f = 0.3. The inset in Figure 2b shows two hyperbolic bands in porous SiC. Artificial materials like this porous SiC are also called hyperbolic metamaterials, and they can also support hyperbolic phonon polaritons.

To calculate the Casimir force, we use the Maxwell electromagnetic stress tensor method. This method treats the electromagnetic field as a kind of pressure on the surfaces. We also use the properties of macroscopic field operators, which describe the field averaged over many atoms. In the end, the Casimir force at zero temperature is

(6) F = −(ℏ/π) Re ∫₀^∞ dω ∫∫ d²k‖ [2πω²/(c² − k‖²)] × { Σp=TE,TM [r1p(ω,k) r2p(ω,k) e^(2idω²/(c² − k‖²)) / (1 − r1p(ω,k) r2p(ω,k) e^(2idω²/(c² − k‖²)))] },

where the integral runs over all electromagnetic modes, that is, over every possible way the field can vibrate. The wave vector component k‖ lies parallel to the x−y plane. The reflection coefficient r1p (or r2p) describes how strongly a wave of type p bounces back from the top (or bottom) sample into the space between the two samples. There are two types of polarization, TE and TM, which describe two different ways the electric field can vibrate. In each model, the top and bottom samples are identical, so r1p equals r2p. We therefore drop the subscripts 1 and 2.

The integral over positive real frequencies ω can run into singularities, points where the calculation breaks down. We avoid all of them by changing the integral from positive real ω to positive imaginary frequency ξ, that is, ω = iξ. The Casimir force can then be written as

(7) F = (ℏ/2π²) ∫₀^∞ dξ ∫₀^∞ k‖ dk‖ [ξ²/(c² + k‖²)] × { Σp=TE,TM [rp(iξ,k) rp(iξ,k) e^(−2dξ²/(c² + k‖²)) / (1 − rp(iξ,k) rp(iξ,k) e^(−2dξ²/(c² + k‖²)))] }.

To calculate the Casimir force, we find the reflection coefficients using the approach described in [51]. In this study, graphene is a single layer, so it can be treated as a sheet that carries a current. Appendix A gives the full working out of rTE and rTM. For a TE-polarized wave, the reflection coefficient of the graphene-covered hyperbolic material is

(8) rTE = (kiz − ktzTE − σ/ωμ0) / (kiz + ktzTE + σ/ωμ0),

where kiz = k0² − k‖² and ktzTE = εxx(k0² − k‖²). The wave vector in free space is k0 = ω/c. Because only εxx appears in rTE, TE-polarized waves cannot excite hyperbolic phonon polaritons.

For a TM-polarized wave, the reflection coefficient is

(9) rTM = (εxx kiz − ktzTM + σkiz ktzTM/ωε0) / (εxx kiz + ktzTM + σkiz ktzTM/ωε0),

where ktzTM = εxx(k0² − k‖²)εxx/εzz. TM-polarized waves can excite hyperbolic phonon polaritons, because both εxx and εzz appear in rTM. The reflection coefficients also depend on the graphene conductivity. This means that surface plasmons on the graphene can couple with the electromagnetic modes of the hyperbolic material, especially hyperbolic phonon polaritons.

The optical properties of the sample can be changed easily by adjusting the Fermi level. The Casimir force usually depends on the surroundings, so it can be controlled by the Fermi level.
parts.results:
3. Results and Discussion

3.1. The Casimir Force Between Graphene-Covered hBN Blocks

Figure 3 shows how the Casimir force between two identical solid blocks of hBN, each covered with graphene, changes with the distance d between them. We calculated this for several values of the Fermi level. To make the results easy to compare, we divided the force by a well-known reference force, F0 = ℏcπ²/240d⁴. This is the Casimir force per unit area between two perfectly conducting plates placed parallel to each other a distance d apart. Because the two blocks have exactly the same electric and magnetic properties, the force is clearly attractive at every distance.

For comparison, we also plotted the force between two identical hBN blocks without graphene, shown as the blue line in Figure 3. Covering the hBN blocks with graphene clearly makes the force larger. As the Fermi level (Ef) rises, the force keeps increasing steadily at every separation distance. When the blocks are very close together, the force hardly depends on the Fermi level, and the curves are steep. When the blocks are far apart, the force depends on the Fermi level, but the curves are gentle. Since the Fermi level can be adjusted, the Casimir force can be controlled flexibly.

Figure 3

The relative Casimir force (the force divided by the reference force F0) plotted against the separation distance d. The blue line shows the force between two identical hBN blocks. The other lines show the force between two graphene-covered hBN blocks at different Fermi levels.

The Casimir force is linked to all the electromagnetic waves that the two samples can support. Equation (6) tells us that these waves are described by the samples' reflection coefficients. So in Figure 4 we plotted the real parts of two reflection coefficients, rTM and rTE, against the frequency ω and the wave vector component k||. The real part is the part of a number that is not imaginary. The two kinds of waves differ in how their electric and magnetic fields are lined up. TM waves have their electric field in the plane of the surface, and TE waves have their electric field at right angles to it.

Comparing Figure 4a with Figure 4b, we see that the TM reflection coefficient of graphene-covered hBN is clearly larger than that of plain hBN whenever the frequency is below 0.1 ω0, for every value of k||. Here ω0 is a reference frequency that sets the scale of the material's response. The TE reflection coefficients in Figure 4c and 4d, however, are hard to tell apart.

Equation (8) explains why. When graphene covers hBN, the TE reflection coefficient depends on the graphene's electrical conductivity σ as well as on the permittivity of hBN, εxx,hBN. Permittivity describes how strongly a material responds to an electric field. Equation (9) shows that the TM reflection coefficient of graphene-covered hBN depends on εxx,hBN, εzz,hBN and σ. Without graphene, it depends only on the permittivity of hBN. So the surface plasmons on the graphene mainly interact with the hyperbolic phonon polaritons on the hBN. This is why covering hBN with graphene makes the Casimir force larger, as Figure 3 shows. For this reason, the rest of our study focuses on how surface plasmons and hyperbolic phonon polaritons interact when they are excited by a TM wave.

Figure 4

The real parts of the TM and TE reflection coefficients, plotted against frequency ω and wave vector component k||. (a) hBN. (b) Graphene-covered hBN with Fermi level Ef = 0.1 eV. (c) hBN. (d) Graphene-covered hBN with Fermi level Ef = 0.1 eV.

To pick out how much surface plasmons and hyperbolic phonon polaritons each add to the extra force, we plotted the TM reflection coefficients against the imaginary frequency ξ and the wave vector component k|| in Figure 5. The imaginary frequency is a mathematical tool that lets us calculate the Casimir force. Comparing Figure 5a with 5b, the TM reflection coefficient of graphene-covered hBN is clearly larger at low frequencies. As Figure 5b–d shows, the area where this happens grows as the Fermi level rises.

In Equation (7), the term exp(−2dξ²/c² + k||²) acts like a cutoff. It keeps only the waves that fit within a certain range. For a separation of d = 1 μm, we drew the edge of this range as a circle, ξ²/c² + k||² = (1/2d)², in Figure 5. The size of the force can be described by the reflection coefficients inside this circle [23]. Clearly, as the Fermi level rises, a larger share of the reflection coefficients inside the circle become large. In the same way, the Casimir force at d = 1 μm grows as the Fermi level rises, as Figure 3 shows.

The radius of this circle is also inversely proportional to the separation distance d, so a smaller gap means a smaller circle. In Figure 5d we also drew the circles for d = 0.5 μm and d = 3 μm. As the distance grows, the circle shrinks, and a larger share of the reflection coefficients inside it are large. As a result, the Casimir force gets closer to the reference force F0 as the distance grows, as Figure 3 shows.

Figure 5

The TM reflection coefficient rTM(iξ) plotted against imaginary frequency ξ and wave vector component k||. (a) hBN. (b–d) Graphene-covered hBN with Fermi levels (b) Ef = 0.1 eV, (c) Ef = 0.5 eV and (d) Ef = 0.9 eV. The solid curves in all panels mark the circle ξ²/c² + k||² = (1/2d)² for d = 1 μm. The dashed and dotted lines in panel (d) mark the cases d = 0.5 μm and d = 3 μm.

3.2. The Casimir Force Between Graphene-Covered Porous SiC

We also studied the Casimir force between two identical solid blocks of porous SiC, each covered with graphene, and how it changes with the separation distance d. We set the filling factor to f = 0.1, meaning the air holes take up 10% of the material. Figure 6a shows the forces for different Fermi levels. For comparison, we also plotted the force between two porous SiC blocks without graphene, shown as the blue line in Figure 6a.

Just as with graphene-covered hBN, the Casimir force keeps increasing steadily as the Fermi level rises, especially when the blocks are far apart. We expected this from our analysis above, because porous SiC is also a hyperbolic material. And when the Fermi level and the separation distance are fixed, the force is larger for graphene-covered porous SiC than for graphene-covered hBN, as Figure 3 shows.

Figure 2b shows that both εxx,p−SiC and εzz,p−SiC, the two parts of the permittivity of porous SiC, are negative between 1.496 ω0 and 1.761 ω0. This means that porous SiC also supports electromagnetic waves other than hyperbolic phonon polaritons. All of these waves interact and add to the Casimir force.

Figure 6

How the Casimir force depends on the separation distance d. (a) The blue line shows two identical porous SiC blocks. The other lines show graphene-covered porous SiC at different Fermi levels. The filling factor is set to f = 0.1. (b) Graphene-covered porous SiC with different filling factors, all at a fixed Fermi level Ef = 0.5 eV.

Porous SiC is an artificial hyperbolic material, and its permittivity can be changed by the filling factor f. So the filling factor affects how the surface plasmons on the graphene interact with the hyperbolic phonon polaritons on the porous SiC, and this lets us control the Casimir force. Figure 6b shows the Casimir force against the separation distance d for different filling factors. As the filling factor increases, the relative force drops sharply at every separation distance.

This result is easy to understand. As the filling factor increases, the share of air holes also increases. According to Equations (4) and (5), the electric properties of porous SiC should weaken as the filling factor increases. So the Casimir force falls as the waves supported by porous SiC contribute less.

Figure 7 shows the permittivity of porous SiC against the imaginary frequency ξ for different filling factors, to support this explanation. As the filling factor increases, both εxx,p−SiC and εzz,p−SiC become smaller at every ξ, which confirms our prediction. Also, when ξ is below ω0, all the curves in Figure 7 are almost flat, but they slope when ξ is between ω0 and 10 ω0. As we mentioned earlier, the force at a small separation comes mainly from waves at high frequencies, while waves at low frequencies mainly add to the force at a large separation [22]. Figure 6b shows this too: the relative force changes steeply when the blocks are close together, but only gently when they are far apart.

Figure 7

(a) εxx,p−SiC and (b) εzz,p−SiC plotted against imaginary frequency ξ for different filling factors f.

3.3. Discussion

At zero temperature, the Casimir force per unit area between two parallel graphene sheets falls off as 1/d⁴, but its size is much smaller than that between two perfectly conducting plates [38]. According to the data in [38], the force between graphene sheets on an area of 1 cm² is about 0.006 F0 = 7.8 × 10⁻⁶ N when d = 0.1 μm. For the same area and distance, Figure 3 gives a force of about 0.145 F0 = 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ N when Ef = 0.1 eV, and Figure 6a gives about 0.197 F0 = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ N. So putting graphene on a hyperbolic material makes the Casimir force more than ten times larger.

For comparison, the Casimir force per 1 cm² between two identical artificial hyperbolic materials is about 0.1 F0 = 8.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ N at d ≈ 2 μm [23]. For the same area and distance, Figure 3 gives about 0.178 F0 = 1.5 × 10⁻⁹ N when Ef = 0.1 eV, and Figure 6a gives about 0.233 F0 = 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ N. Covering a hyperbolic material with a single layer of graphene therefore makes the Casimir force larger.

Our samples sit in free space, so a real experiment would need a high-vacuum chamber to measure the Casimir force between graphene-covered hyperbolic materials. The quality of the graphene layer should also be checked to make sure it is just one atom thick. The way the Casimir force changes with distance could be measured with the experimental setup described in [7].

However, there are some problems. One difficulty is that it is very hard to keep two flat samples parallel to each other over small distances. Most experiments instead make one of the samples a ball with a large radius, so the shape of the samples affects the size of the Casimir force. Another issue is temperature, since we worked at zero temperature. The Casimir force at a real, non-zero temperature can be found by replacing the integral over the imaginary frequency ξ in Equation (7) with a sum over Matsubara frequencies, a set of evenly spaced values used for calculations at finite temperature [24]. The effects of sample shape and of non-zero temperature on the Casimir force of our proposal still need further study.
